claims.text: Controlled aging can induce a coherent L12-ordered secondary phase in an fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti high-entropy alloy.
The proposed L12 precipitates will be Ti-rich.
Coherent L12 precipitates can coexist with a high-entropy fcc matrix without eliminating the fcc matrix.
The single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti baseline has coercivity below 100 Oe.
The low coercivity of the baseline is caused by suppressed orbital moments resulting from high configurational entropy and chemical disorder.
The fcc matrix and L12 precipitates will remain stable over 300-600 K.
Coherent L12 precipitates create local lattice-strain fields in the surrounding fcc matrix.
The L12 precipitates act as magnetic-domain-wall pinning centers.
Precipitate-induced strain and chemical ordering lift d-orbital degeneracy in the adjacent fcc matrix.
Lifting the d-orbital degeneracy restores an orbital magnetic-moment contribution to magnetic anisotropy.
Precipitate-matrix interfaces increase the energy barrier for magnetization reversal through domain-wall pinning.
Introducing a second phase or changing chemical interactions can increase coercivity in a high-entropy alloy.
The dual-phase alloy will exhibit coercivity exceeding 100 Oe at elevated temperatures.
The saturation magnetization of the dual-phase alloy will remain comparable to that of the single-phase baseline.
Formation of incoherent BCC or B2 phases would degrade mechanical integrity or magnetic coupling.
A precipitate volume fraction above a percolation threshold would magnetically isolate regions of the alloy.
Comparing otherwise matched single-phase and aged dual-phase samples over 300-600 K can distinguish their magnetic contributions.
The hypothesis is falsified if the confirmed dual-phase sample has coercivity statistically indistinguishable from or below that of the single-phase control at every tested temperature.

contradictions.description: The operating regime is described as significantly above room temperature, but the stated 300-600 K range includes 300 K, which is approximately room temperature.
